title: Podcast with Rob Jesudason, CEO and Founder of Serendipity Capital - Quantum Computing Report
gist: Rob Jesudason, CEO of the $1.3B permanent-capital vehicle Serendipity Capital (Quantinuum, Monarch Quantum, Delta g, QuantX), argues quantum investing requires triangulating across experts because modalities are like religion, the industry is shifting from lab science to managerial and engineering scale, governments should be the last check not the first, and smaller nations should aim to be fastest integrators rather than innovators.

insights.claim: Serendipity Capital is a $1.3 billion permanent capital vehicle, structured as a company whose investors become shareholders rather than a fund with a deploy-or-exit window, and has invested in quantum consistently since its 2019 inception.
insights.speaker: Rob Jesudason
insights.so_what: Permanent-capital structure lets the firm hold quantum bets across long, uncertain development timelines without forced exits.
insights.quote: we're not a fund, we're a permanent capital vehicle... when people invest in us or give us money, they become shareholders in a company versus unit holders in a fund.

insights.claim: Serendipity is the sixth largest shareholder in Quantinuum, having gone on the cap table in 2020 and invested in every round through the IPO, and also holds Monarch Quantum (photonic laser light engines), Delta g (quantum sensing), QuantX (atomic clocks), Emergence Quantum, and BlueQubit.
insights.speaker: Rob Jesudason
insights.so_what: A broad cross-modality portfolio reveals where a sophisticated permanent-capital investor is placing quantum bets.

insights.claim: Photonic lasers typically represent 35 to 50 percent of the bill of materials of a quantum computer, which is why Serendipity invested in Monarch Quantum as a multimodality control-layer component.
insights.speaker: Rob Jesudason
insights.so_what: High BOM share flags photonic laser supply as a potential high-value chokepoint across modalities.
insights.quote: It's typically 35 to 50 percent of the bill of materials of a quantum computer.

insights.claim: Evaluating quantum companies requires triangulating across many experts because modalities function like religion, with each believer convinced theirs is the correct path and rarely conceding a rival modality could be better.
insights.speaker: Rob Jesudason
insights.so_what: Investors should distrust any single-modality advocate and build a cross-expert ecosystem before committing capital.
insights.quote: I always compare modalities to religion. Everyone believes there's a God, but they believe they're right.

insights.claim: Serendipity's house view is that the future is multimodality with two or three of the seven modalities becoming pivotal in the next three to five years, naming neutral atom as a likely winner and citing QuEra, and also expressing belief in trapped ion.
insights.speaker: Rob Jesudason
insights.so_what: Names specific modality winners a major investor is backing, useful for benchmarking modality bets.

insights.claim: Control-systems players may become multimodality oligopolists or monopolists, making the systems and control-system layer more investable than the frequently over-focused hardware side.
insights.speaker: Rob Jesudason
insights.so_what: Points investors toward the control-systems layer as a defensible, cross-modality profit pool.
insights.quote: I think there are going to be control systems players that are going to be multimodality, and they're going to be oligopolists or monopolists in that area.

insights.claim: There has been negative selection in quantum companies that went public via SPAC, whereas Quantinuum did a formal IPO with long-only and strategic support, differentiated partly because its largest shareholder Honeywell was itself breaking up as a public company.
insights.speaker: Rob Jesudason
insights.so_what: Frames IPO-route quantum names as higher quality than SPAC-route ones for public investors screening the sector.
insights.quote: rightly or wrongly, there's been a little bit of negative selection in the people who've gone to SPAC.

insights.claim: The future of quantum is fewer SPACs and more companies doing formal IPOs with institutional and strategic capital bases, so the sector trades with less volatility and long-term support rather than trading like crypto.
insights.speaker: Rob Jesudason
insights.so_what: Predicts a maturation that would reduce momentum-driven volatility in quantum equities.
insights.quote: I don't think it's particularly good for quantum to trade like crypto. The future for quantum is for it to trade with less volatility.

insights.claim: Retail investors find it almost impossible to choose quantum stocks because a gap between promotional PowerPoint presentations and unread technical white papers drives narrative-based momentum trading and volatility.
insights.speaker: Rob Jesudason
insights.so_what: The narrative-vs-physics gap explains quantum-stock volatility and warns retail against narrative-driven entries.
insights.quote: certain companies in the quantum industry have slightly done themselves a disservice by creating a gap between the PowerPoint presentations that people will read and the white papers that a lot of non-technical people don't read.

insights.claim: The quantum industry is shifting from lab-driven science to managerial execution and engineering scale, so teams now need as much operational talent as physics talent to ship one system and then several systems.
insights.speaker: Rob Jesudason
insights.so_what: Signals investors should weight management and engineering-scale capability, not just physics, when picking quantum winners.
insights.quote: we're entering the phase of managerial execution and engineering scale... That is tens of thousands of engineering hours.

insights.claim: Serendipity has been slow and selective on quantum software and algorithm companies, admitting it should have invested in Classiq when it looked in 2020-2022, while flagging Phasecraft as an interesting non-portfolio algorithm company.
insights.speaker: Rob Jesudason
insights.so_what: Indicates the software/algorithm layer is still early but becoming more interesting as hardware quality rises.
insights.quote: if I kick myself on one investment we should have done that we didn't do, it was Classiq.

insights.claim: Governments should avoid being the first investor in quantum companies and instead partner with private capital later as validators, because governments too often are the first check picking wrong companies and propping up firms private capital won't fund.
insights.speaker: Rob Jesudason
insights.so_what: A policy prescription that private-led funding, with government as last check, better identifies scalable winners.
insights.quote: You shouldn't aim to be the first check. You should be the last check.

insights.claim: The US leaders across modalities were primarily private-sector funded with DARPA grants only on the edge, with government coming in at latter stages, contrasted with continental Europe examples where governments back companies private capital rejects.
insights.speaker: Rob Jesudason
insights.so_what: Frames private-led funding as the driver of US quantum leadership, a template for allocation policy.

insights.claim: Countries without the scale to build a leading hardware stack, such as Australia, Canada, or Singapore, are better off becoming the fastest integrators of winning technologies and building software or use-case ecosystems around imported hardware rather than trying to be the innovators.
insights.speaker: Rob Jesudason
insights.so_what: A sovereignty framework suggesting smaller nations invest in domain software (e.g. mining) leveraging US hardware.
insights.quote: there's a set of countries that should realistically aim not to be the innovators, but the fastest integrators of the winning technologies into their economies.

insights.claim: UK companies Cambridge Quantum and Oxford Ionics are cited as good companies that ended up as parts of large US companies, illustrating the risk that undercapitalized national champions get absorbed abroad.
insights.speaker: Rob Jesudason
insights.so_what: Illustrates capital scarcity risk driving national quantum assets into foreign ownership.
insights.quote: Cambridge Quantum and Oxford Ionics are good examples of good companies that ended up being part of large US companies today.
